description: Dynamic equilibrium, Le Chatelier's principle and applying it to the Haber process conditions.
content_html:
Reversible Reactions

Most chemical reactions go to completion — the reactants are used up and only products remain. However, some reactions are reversible. In a reversible reaction, the products can react to re-form the original reactants. This is shown using the equilibrium symbol \(\rightleftharpoons\) instead of a single arrow.

A well-known example is the dehydration of hydrated copper sulfate: blue hydrated copper sulfate (\(CuSO_4 \cdot 5H_2O\)) loses water when heated to form white anhydrous copper sulfate (\(CuSO_4\)). Adding water to the white powder restores the blue colour. Another example is the decomposition of ammonium chloride: \(NH_4Cl(s) \rightleftharpoons NH_3(g) + HCl(g)\). When heated, it decomposes into gases; when cooled, the gases recombine to form solid ammonium chloride again.

Key Fact

In a reversible reaction, if the forward reaction is exothermic, the reverse reaction is endothermic by the same amount of energy. The two energy changes are equal in magnitude but opposite in sign.

Reversible reactions are significant in many biological and industrial contexts. The reaction between haemoglobin and oxygen in the blood is reversible: at the lungs, where oxygen concentration is high, haemoglobin combines with oxygen to form oxyhaemoglobin; at the tissues, where oxygen concentration is low, the reverse reaction releases oxygen to the cells. This is a natural example of Le Chatelier’s principle operating in a biological system — the equilibrium position shifts depending on the local conditions. Understanding reversibility is essential for designing efficient chemical manufacturing processes, because it helps chemists choose conditions that maximise the yield of the desired product while minimising energy use and waste.

Dynamic Equilibrium

When a reversible reaction takes place in a closed system, a dynamic equilibrium is eventually reached. At equilibrium:

  • The rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction.
  • The concentrations of reactants and products remain constant (but are not necessarily equal to each other).
  • Both reactions are still occurring at the molecular level — this is why the equilibrium is described as “dynamic.”

Equilibrium does not mean the amounts of reactants and products are equal — it means they are constant. The equilibrium position can strongly favour the products or the reactants. Equilibrium is not a static state — both forward and reverse reactions continue, but at equal rates, so the net composition does not change. Equilibrium can only be reached in a closed system; if products escape, the reaction continues in the forward direction until completion.

The position of equilibrium — how far the reaction proceeds towards products — is described qualitatively. We say the equilibrium “lies to the right” if products predominate, or “lies to the left” if reactants predominate. In many industrial reactions, chemists deliberately choose conditions that push the equilibrium position as far to the right as possible while keeping the rate acceptable. This involves an understanding of both kinetics (rate) and thermodynamics (equilibrium) working together, which is why industrial chemistry is a careful balancing act between speed and yield.

Le Chatelier’s Principle (Higher Tier)

Le Chatelier’s principle states that if the conditions of a system at equilibrium are changed, the equilibrium position shifts in the direction that opposes the change. This allows us to predict how temperature, concentration, and pressure affect the yield of a reaction.

Temperature: Increasing temperature shifts the equilibrium in the endothermic direction (to absorb the extra heat). Decreasing temperature shifts it in the exothermic direction. This changes the yield of the reaction.

Concentration: Increasing the concentration of a reactant shifts equilibrium towards the products (to use up the extra reactant). Increasing the concentration of a product shifts it towards the reactants. Removing a product also shifts equilibrium to the right (towards products).

Pressure (reactions involving gases): Increasing pressure shifts equilibrium towards the side with fewer moles of gas (to reduce the pressure). Decreasing pressure shifts it towards the side with more moles of gas. Count the total moles of gas on each side to predict the direction of shift.

Catalyst: A catalyst does not change the equilibrium position — it speeds up both forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached faster but the final proportions of reactants and products are unchanged. This is a frequently tested distinction.

The Haber Process: A Le Chatelier’s Example

The Haber process is the most important industrial application of Le Chatelier’s principle. It produces ammonia, which is essential for making fertilisers, explosives and cleaning products:

$$N_2(g) + 3H_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NH_3(g) \quad \Delta H = -92 \text{ kJ/mol}$$

The forward reaction is exothermic and there are 4 moles of gas on the left and 2 moles on the right. Applying Le Chatelier’s principle: a lower temperature favours the exothermic direction (more ammonia), but the rate would be unacceptably slow. A higher pressure favours the side with fewer moles of gas (the products), increasing yield, but very high pressures are dangerous and expensive to maintain.

Key Fact

Industrial conditions are a compromise: approximately 450°C (high enough for acceptable rate, low enough for reasonable yield), approximately 200 atm (high yield without excessive cost and safety risks), and an iron catalyst (increases rate without changing yield). Unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen are recycled through the reactor to maximise efficiency.
exam_tip_html: In questions on equilibrium, always be precise: ‘the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant’ is correct; ‘the concentrations are equal’ is wrong. For Le Chatelier’s principle questions, work through the logic step by step: identify what has changed → state which direction the equilibrium shifts → explain why using Le Chatelier’s principle. A very common error is stating that a catalyst shifts the equilibrium position — it does not; it only speeds up the rate at which equilibrium is reached. Higher Tier: in Haber process questions, always explain that the industrial conditions are a compromise between yield and rate, and cost and safety — not the theoretically optimal conditions for yield alone.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Reversible reactions can proceed in both directions. In a closed system, a dynamic equilibrium is reached when the rates of forward and reverse reactions are equal and concentrations of reactants and products are constant (not necessarily equal). Both reactions still occur at the molecular level.
  • Higher: Le Chatelier’s principle — if conditions change, the equilibrium shifts to oppose the change. Increasing temperature favours the endothermic direction; increasing pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules; increasing reactant concentration shifts equilibrium towards products. Catalysts do not change the equilibrium position.
  • The Haber process (N&sub2; + 3H&sub2; ⇌ 2NH&sub3;) uses conditions of approximately 450°C, 200 atm, and an iron catalyst — a compromise between yield, rate, cost and safety. Unreacted gases are recycled.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes the state of dynamic equilibrium?
A) The forward and reverse reactions have stopped
B) The concentrations of reactants and products are equal
C) The rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction
D) Only the forward reaction is occurring
practice_questions.marks: C) The rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the three conditions used in the Haber process.
practice_questions.marks: Approximately 450°C; approximately 200 atm (high pressure); iron catalyst. [1 mark — all three required]

practice_questions.text: Describe what happens to a system at equilibrium when a product is removed from the reaction mixture.
practice_questions.marks: Removing a product reduces its concentration [1 mark]; the equilibrium shifts in the forward direction (towards products) to replace the product that has been removed [1 mark].

practice_questions.text:
The Haber process reaction is: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) (forward reaction exothermic).

Explain why a low temperature increases the yield of ammonia but is not used industrially.
practice_questions.marks: A low temperature favours the exothermic direction (forward reaction) because Le Chatelier's principle states the equilibrium shifts to release heat and oppose the cooling [1 mark]; this increases the proportion of ammonia at equilibrium (greater yield) [1 mark]; however, a very low temperature slows the rate of reaction so dramatically that the time taken to reach equilibrium becomes commercially unacceptable [1 mark].

practice_questions.text:
The reaction between sulfur dioxide and oxygen is: 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g)

The forward reaction is exothermic. Predict and explain the effect of each of the following changes on the equilibrium position:
(a) Increasing pressure [2 marks]
(b) Increasing temperature [2 marks]
practice_questions.marks: (a) Increasing pressure shifts equilibrium towards the side with fewer moles of gas [1 mark]; the products side has 2 moles of gas vs 3 moles on the reactants side, so equilibrium shifts to the right / more SO₃ is produced [1 mark]; (b) Increasing temperature shifts equilibrium in the endothermic direction (reverse reaction) to absorb the extra heat [1 mark]; equilibrium shifts to the left / yield of SO₃ decreases [1 mark].

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the industrial conditions for the Haber process (approximately 450°C, 200 atm, iron catalyst) represent a compromise, rather than the conditions that would give the maximum theoretical yield of ammonia.

In your answer, consider the effects of temperature, pressure and the catalyst separately.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Temperature — lowering temperature favours the exothermic forward reaction and gives a higher equilibrium yield of NH₃, but rate becomes too slow at very low temperatures; 450°C is a compromise giving acceptable rate and yield; increasing temperature increases rate but reduces yield. Pressure — higher pressure favours the side with fewer moles of gas (products: 2 mol vs reactants: 4 mol) so gives higher yield and rate, but very high pressures are extremely expensive to achieve and maintain and present safety hazards; 200 atm is a compromise. Catalyst — the iron catalyst increases the rate at which equilibrium is reached (both forward and reverse equally) without affecting the equilibrium position or yield; it is used to compensate for the rate reduction caused by the moderate temperature. Unreacted gases recycled to improve overall efficiency.
Secure: All three factors addressed correctly; compromise nature of conditions stated for at least two; catalyst correctly identified as not affecting yield.
Developing: Temperature and pressure discussed; catalyst mentioned; compromise language used for one factor.
Emerging: One or two conditions named; limited explanation of compromise.

knowledge_checks.q: What does Le Chatelier's principle state about a system at equilibrium that is subjected to a change?
options: The equilibrium shifts to maximise the concentration of products
The equilibrium shifts to oppose the change

knowledge_checks.q: For the Haber process N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, increasing pressure shifts the equilibrium to the right. Why?
options: There are fewer moles of gas on the right-hand side
Nitrogen and hydrogen are more reactive under pressure
The catalyst works better at high pressure

knowledge_checks.q: At dynamic equilibrium, the rate of the forward reaction _____ the rate of the reverse reaction.
In the Haber process, an iron _____ is used to speed up the rate at which equilibrium is reached, without changing the equilibrium position.
Match each change to its effect on the equilibrium N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ (exothermic forward reaction):
right: No change in equilibrium position — faster to reach equilibrium

flashcard_questions.a: A reaction that can proceed in both the forward and reverse directions.
A state in a closed system where forward and reverse reaction rates are equal and concentrations remain constant.

flashcard_questions.q: Does equilibrium mean reactant and product concentrations are equal?
flashcard_questions.a: No — it means they are constant, not necessarily equal.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Le Chatelier's principle state?
flashcard_questions.a: If conditions change, the equilibrium shifts to oppose the change.

flashcard_questions.q: If the forward reaction is exothermic, which direction does the equilibrium shift when temperature is increased?
flashcard_questions.a: Left (towards reactants) — the endothermic direction absorbs the extra heat.

flashcard_questions.q: In the Haber process equation N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, why does increasing pressure favour the products?
flashcard_questions.a: There are fewer moles of gas on the right (2) than the left (4), so high pressure shifts equilibrium right.

flashcard_questions.q: What are the approximate conditions used in the Haber process?
Why is 450°C used in the Haber process rather than a lower temperature?
flashcard_questions.a: A lower temperature would give a higher yield but the rate would be too slow — 450°C is a compromise.

flashcard_questions.q: Does a catalyst shift the equilibrium position?
flashcard_questions.a: No — it speeds up both forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached faster but yield is unchanged.

flashcard_questions.q: What happens to unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen in the Haber process?
flashcard_questions.a: They are recycled back through the reactor to improve efficiency.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the energy change of the forward reaction in the Haber process?
flashcard_questions.a: Exothermic — it releases energy (the ΔH value is negative).

glossary_terms.definition: A reaction that can proceed in both the forward and reverse directions, shown by the equilibrium symbol ⇌.
A system in which matter cannot enter or leave, so no reactants or products can escape.
A state reached in a closed system when the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction, so the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant.
The relative amounts of reactants and products at equilibrium; it can favour the products (more products) or reactants (more reactants) depending on conditions.
If the conditions of a system at equilibrium are changed, the equilibrium position shifts to oppose the change and partially counteract it.
The industrial process for manufacturing ammonia by reacting nitrogen and hydrogen gases under high temperature and pressure with an iron catalyst.
